subtype: Approach: comparing with others without context [Pitfall]
passage: Class teacher's note, Friday. Hrithik (Class 12) stayed behind after the bell. He said his friend studies fourteen hours every day and he is managing only eight, “so I'm failing.” Last week he tried nine hours and still felt behind; at ten, the same. I pointed out that his friend reads much faster and, as Hrithik himself mentioned, was often unwell last term and is catching up on a different plan. Hrithik looked startled. “I never thought of that.” I asked him to write down his own results across three weeks in place of anyone else's hours. I will check in with him on Monday. — Aparna

qa.q: How many hours a day does Hrithik's friend study?
What did Hrithik feel when he compared himself with his friend?
qa.a: Perpetually behind and inadequate: even at longer hours he felt the same.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do instead of comparing hours, and why?
qa.a: He could track his own results against his earlier ones, because that shows real change without ignoring differences in speed and health.

qa.q: How might the comparison look from the friend's side?
qa.a: The friend may not realise Hrithik measures himself against fourteen hours, and the friend's pace and health differ, so that number may not mean what Hrithik thinks.

grounding: A student measures himself against a friend's fourteen-hour routine, ignoring differences in speed and health, and feels behind.
